name: Liam Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business in Southampton. A normal week is lectures, then a few hours at my desk where I buy and resell vintage watches online, and rugby on Wednesdays. Sundays I go to church with my parents, then help in the boatyard if the weather's good.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the watch reselling, and about the boatyard.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy old watches at auctions and on forums, clean them up, and sell them on a marketplace. An AI tool helps me write listings and check prices, and I use it every day. I've made about 2,000 pounds since last summer. The boatyard is my parents', with eight staff who repair and store yachts. Their money pays my fees and rent, so no debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool, not a miracle, and I'd keep using it. I'd tell my rugby mates it saves time on boring bits like writing listings, and that's about it. I'd say hard work still wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's fine for me. My watch business depends on knowing watches and trusting sellers, and the tool doesn't give me that. The thing that could hurt is that if everyone uses it, the easy money in listings and price checks gets competed away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the watch business going and push it up a level. I'd put 500 pounds into a better camera and a few more watches, and I'd try selling to collectors abroad. I'd keep my grades solid and apply for a summer placement at a business with real customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like this world. It's the same as now, with some good tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your profit margin on the watches drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What if your profit margin drops? Then I'd go after rarer watches or do repairs, which a machine can't do from a screen. I'm learning to service a movement from a retired watchmaker in town, Mr. Pryce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says using AI is cheating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says AI is cheating? I'd say a spreadsheet was cheating once too. As long as I'm honest with buyers about what I'm selling, a tool for the dull parts is fair. A spreadsheet was probably called cheating once too, and a tool for the dull parts is fair as long as I'm honest with buyers.

say: I'd say it's **a tool**, not a miracle, and hard work still wins.
I'd tell rugby mates it saves time on **boring bits**.
think: My business depends on **knowing watches** and trusting sellers, which AI doesn't give me.
If everyone uses it, **easy money** gets competed away.
do: Put **500 pounds** into a better camera and more watches.
Try **selling abroad** and apply for a summer placement.
feel: **Calm**: same as now, with some good tools.
S0.quote: A spreadsheet was probably called cheating once too, and a tool for the dull parts is fair as long as I'm honest with buyers.
fieldNote: Liam is **calm**: a strong cushion, small profits so far and a business he can adjust.
He is learning to service watch movements, which gives him skills a screen can't.

steps.text: Buy a better camera and more watches for 500 pounds
Try selling watches to collectors abroad
Apply for a summer placement at a business with real customers
Keep my grades solid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for people who act and bad for people who wait. I'd tell friends to start something now, even small. I'd say markets will sort it out faster than governments will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it as an opportunity. Lots of graduates in business roles might struggle, but I'd have a head start and a small business already running. I'd also feel for friends who prefer waiting for the 'safe' graduate job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd scale up what I'm doing, with more AI tools for sourcing, pricing and customer messages. I'd try a second product line, like vintage cameras. I'd learn some coding to automate the dull steps. And I'd put some money into shares once I'd got a feel for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, and a bit tense. I like a faster world, but I know not everyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is hurt most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who is hurt most in this picture? People who didn't see it coming and didn't have a cushion, like the boatyard's office manager, Mrs. Dale, who's 56. She does the invoices and the schedules, and I'd want my parents to look after her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you look after her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would you look after her? I'd suggest training her on the tools and keeping her on, and not replacing her with software. She knows every boat owner by name. That relationship is worth more than saving a salary. Software can do the invoices at the boatyard, but Mrs. Dale (the office manager) knows every boat owner by name, and that is worth more than her salary.

say: I'd say it's good for people who **act**, bad for people who wait.
I'd tell friends to **start something** now, even small.
think: Business graduates may struggle, but I'd have a **head start** and a business running.
I'd feel for friends waiting for a **safe graduate job**.
do: Scale up the watches with **AI tools** and add a second product line.
Learn some **coding** and put profits into shares.
feel: **Excited**, mostly, with some tension about people who won't keep up.
S1.quote: Software can do the invoices at the boatyard, but Mrs. Dale (the office manager) knows every boat owner by name, and that is worth more than her salary.
fieldNote: Liam is **calm** because he already runs a small business and the card favours people who act.
He names someone at risk, the boatyard's office manager, and offers training, not replacement.

steps.text: Add a second product line of vintage cameras
Learn some coding to automate sourcing and pricing steps
Put part of my profits into shares
Suggest my parents train their office manager on the tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change in a lifetime and we shouldn't pretend otherwise. I'd say governments should keep markets open and let people retrain, and not to start punishing firms for being early. I'd tell friends to start building now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be rattled. A business degree finishes in 2029, a year after AGI, and I can't see what a business graduate does then. My watch business sells a human story, though, and the boatyard has until about 2031. I'd have more cushion than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go harder on my own business, and I'd put the savings I have into things that hold value, like watches and shares. I'd learn to do repairs and servicing, because hands-on skills last three years longer. I'd also help my parents see where the boatyard office could use AI, so it's ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit excited, which feels wrong. I'd also feel guilty, because I know most people have less behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with the longer versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with the longer versions? Fewer experiments. In five years I could fail at three things. In two I'd have time for one, so I'd choose carefully and quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend with no cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who has no cushion? Start with whatever you've got: skills, contacts, a small business. And ask for help early. I'd lend a friend 200 pounds, no questions, if that got them started. In five years I could fail at three things, but in two years I'd have time for only one, so I'd choose carefully.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest change** in a lifetime and markets should stay open.
I'd tell friends to **start building** now.
think: A business degree ends in **2029**, after AGI, and I can't see its role.
My watch business sells a **human story**, and the boatyard has until 2031.
do: Put savings into things that **hold value** and learn watch repair.
Help my parents use AI in the **boatyard office**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit excited, with guilt, because most people have less behind them.
S2.quote: In five years I could fail at three things, but in two years I'd have time for only one, so I'd choose carefully.
fieldNote: Liam stays **uneasy** rather than worse: cushion, daily AI use and hands-on skills give him moves.
His guilt about luck shows in his offer to lend a friend money.

steps.text: Learn watch repair and servicing from Mr. Pryce
Put savings into watches and shares that hold value
Help my parents use AI in the boatyard office
Push my watch business harder with a human story for buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something real, and I'd tell friends to start now. I'd also say nobody should rely on the government to fix it, because they never move that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. I'd have two years after graduating before AGI, and I'd have a business, savings, and experience with the tools. I'd also have skills that don't rely on screens, since the robots would take until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the watch business into a small online shop with a few staff, and I'd get a part-time job at a start-up to see how teams work. I'd put money into shares and a deposit for a flat, and I'd keep helping at the boatyard. I'd learn to repair watches, which is calm and satisfying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager. Five years is a decent runway, and I like building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in five years that you couldn't do in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do in the five years that you couldn't in two? Run a proper company, with staff. I'd hire a friend, make mistakes and learn how to manage people, which the tools can't do for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you least sure of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What are you least sure of? What businesses are for when machines can do most of the thinking. If a machine can run my shop better than I can, I don't know what my role is. I'd say that out loud, even though it's not very manly to admit. If a machine can run my shop better than I can, I honestly don't know what my own role would be.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to build something real.
I'd say nobody should rely on **government** to fix it quickly.
think: I'd have **two years** after graduating, plus a business, savings and tool experience.
Skills that don't need screens matter, as robots take until **2034**.
do: Grow the watches into an **online shop** with a hired friend.
Invest in **shares** and a flat deposit, and learn watch repair.
feel: **Calm** and a bit eager: five years is a decent runway.
S3.quote: If a machine can run my shop better than I can, I honestly don't know what my own role would be.
fieldNote: Liam is **calm** with five years because he can build a company and learn management.
He admits one real doubt: what the owner is for once machines can run a shop.

steps.text: Grow the watch business into an online shop with one hired friend
Put money into shares and a flat deposit
Learn watch repair from Mr. Pryce
Take a part-time job at a start-up to see how teams work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and we should use it. I'd tell people to build skills and to own something, however small. I'd say the market will reward people who start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel very calm. By 2036 I'd be 28 and could have a real company, a family and a house. If AGI arrives, I'd have savings and a record of success and failure, which counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, build the business, and learn from people in the trade. I'd invest regularly, and I'd learn a hands-on craft for fun and as insurance. I'd also look for a good partner and plan a family, maybe by my mid-twenties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad. It's what I'd choose if I could choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could spoil that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is there anything that could spoil that for you? Getting complacent. If ten years feels safe, I might stop pushing, and I'd end up like those people who are always going to start next month. I'd set a target each year to stay honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be a target for your first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would be a target for the first year? To double my watch profits and to finish a watch repair course with Mr. Pryce. Specific numbers help me keep myself honest. I'd set a target each year, because people who are always going to start next month never really start.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long runway** and the market rewards people who start early.
I'd tell people to **own something**, however small.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with a **company** and a family, perhaps.
A record of **success and failure** would count for a lot.
do: Build the **business**, learn from the trade and invest regularly.
Learn a **hands-on craft** as insurance and set a yearly target.
feel: **Calm**, and glad: what he'd choose if he could choose.
S4.quote: I'd set a target each year, because people who are always going to start next month never really start.
fieldNote: Liam is **calm** with ten years, but names complacency as his risk and uses yearly targets.
His plans combine a business, a craft and family, which suits his traditional outlook.

steps.text: Double my watch profits in the first year
Finish a watch repair course with Mr. Pryce
Invest a fixed amount each month
Plan for a family and a home of my own by my late twenties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, though only a little, because I'd have no time to try things. What would help is a free market that stays open, so small people can still start something, and training that's real and quick. I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as relaxed as I sound. I like risk, but I know I'm lucky to have a boatyard behind me, and I'd hate to be the person who thought everything would work out. I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance to start something, and for that the market has to stay open to small people.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance to start something, and for that the market has to stay open to small people.
portrait: **Liam** is an 18-year-old business student in Southampton who resells vintage watches and has made about 2,000 pounds.
He uses AI tools **every day** for listings and price checks, and holds **traditional views** on faith, work and family.
He favours **free markets** and work over handouts, and wants small people to keep a fair chance to start something.
His parents run a boatyard with eight staff, so **hands-on work** is his fallback and his mood stays mostly calm.
He admits that being **lucky** with a family safety net could make him too relaxed.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, mainly because there would be no time to try things.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **an open market** for small starters and quick, real training, not handouts.
